summary: In Gentile country near Tyre, Jesus tests a mother pleading for her demon-possessed daughter, praises her humble, persistent faith, and heals the girl from a distance.
key_insight: Mark tells this story right after Jesus taught that food cannot make a person unclean. Jesus then walks into “unclean” Gentile land, and a Gentile mother answers Him with an argument about bread. She did not dispute Israel’s place at the table; she trusted there was enough in Jesus for a crumb to reach her.
story: Jesus went from there to the region of Tyre and Sidon. He entered a house and wanted no one to know it, but He could not be hidden. {Mk}

A woman of Canaan from that region came and cried out to Him, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David! My daughter is severely demon-possessed.” {Mt} She was a Greek, a Syro-Phoenician by birth. {Mk} But Jesus answered her not a word. His disciples came and urged Him, “Send her away, for she cries out after us.” He answered, “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” {Mt}

Then she came and fell at His feet {Mk} and worshiped Him, saying, “Lord, help me!” {Mt} Jesus said to her, “Let the children be filled first, for it is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs.” {Mk}

She answered, “Yes, Lord, yet even the little dogs eat the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.” {Mt} Then Jesus said to her, “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be to you as you desire.” {Mt} “For this saying go your way; the demon has gone out of your daughter.” {Mk}
Her daughter was healed from that very hour. {Mt} When the woman reached her house, she found the demon gone and her daughter lying on the bed. {Mk}
differences: Matthew calls her “a woman of Canaan”; Mark calls her “a Greek, a Syro-Phoenician by birth.”
Only Matthew records her cry to the “Son of David,” Jesus’ silence, the disciples’ request and the saying about “the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
Only Mark records “Let the children be filled first” and the woman finding her daughter lying on the bed.
In Matthew Jesus praises her “great” faith; in Mark He says, “For this saying go your way.”

fit.question: Was the woman a Canaanite (Matthew) or a Greek and a Syro-Phoenician (Mark)?

points.label: Three true labels
points.text: “Greek” in Mark means a Gentile, probably a Greek-speaking one. “Syro-Phoenician” names her people: Phoenicians living in the Roman province of Syria. “Canaan” is the old biblical name for those same coastal people; Scripture says Sidon was Canaan’s firstborn (Genesis 10:15, 19).

points.label: Words for different readers
points.text: Mark uses the terms his Roman readers would know. Matthew, writing for readers who knew Israel’s Scriptures, uses the ancient name of Israel’s old enemies, which makes her cry to the “Son of David” all the more striking.

fit.note: The two writers describe one woman with different, accurate labels.
fit.short: Both are true. The Phoenicians descended from the Canaanites; Mark uses the Roman-era name, Matthew the biblical one.

scene.label: Tyre and Sidon
scene.text: These old Phoenician ports lay on the Mediterranean coast north of Galilee, wealthy Gentile cities that Israel’s prophets had often condemned (Ezekiel 26–28). Jesus had said that if they had seen His mighty works, “they would have repented long ago” (Matthew 11:21).

scene.label: Elijah’s widow
scene.text: Centuries earlier, God sent Elijah to a Gentile widow in Zarephath, “which belongs to Sidon” (1 Kings 17:9), and her son was restored to life. Jesus had used her as an example in Nazareth (Luke 4:25–26).

scene.label: “Little dogs”
scene.text: Jews sometimes called Gentiles dogs, meaning the wild scavengers of the streets. Jesus uses a word for little dogs, household pets that stay near the table. The woman takes up His word and builds her answer on it.

scene.label: The children first
scene.text: God’s plan began with Israel and reached outward to the nations. Paul would later describe the gospel as “for the Jew first and also for the Greek” (Romans 1:16). Mark’s word “first” leaves room for the Gentiles’ turn.

witnesses.matthew: Draws out the test: silence, the disciples’ impatience, and the limit of His mission to Israel. Matthew, who names Gentile women such as Rahab and Ruth in Jesus’ family line (1:5) and ends with “all the nations” (28:19), shows a Canaanite calling Jesus “Son of David” and receiving praise for great faith.
witnesses.mark: Places the story right after the teaching on clean and unclean (7:1–23), so Jesus’ words about food are followed by His mercy to a Gentile. Mark alone keeps the word “first,” which leaves room for the Gentiles, and the quiet ending at her house.

seeing.reveals: Jesus came first to Israel, yet His mercy was never meant to stop at Israel’s borders. He let this woman’s faith be tested, and then He held it up as great, a Gentile mother set before His own disciples as an example.
seeing.living: She accepted every word Jesus said about her and still asked. Faith does not argue for its own worthiness; it holds on to His goodness. When He seems silent, keep coming closer, as she did, with the shortest prayer in the story: “Lord, help me!”
seeing.ponder: Are you willing to come to Jesus with nothing to claim but His mercy, and to keep asking when He seems silent?

preaching.big_idea: Faith that claims nothing but Jesus’ mercy finds even His crumbs enough.
preaching.watch_for: Matthew shows three barriers: Jesus’ silence (15:23), His mission to Israel (15:24) and the children’s bread (15:26). She meets each by coming closer. Like the centurion (8:10), the only other person in Matthew whose faith Jesus calls great, she is a Gentile.
